items.headline: OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets and pressure on shared suppliers
items.body: OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple on Friday in federal court in San Jose, bringing federal trade-secret claims plus California claims for contract interference and unfair competition, and naming three files it says Apple obtained: "structure.zip," "CPK_GRR.zip" and "Color Data Template Resin (2).xlsx." It also alleges Apple pressured hardware suppliers the two companies share, in one case confining OpenAI's work to night shifts and in another inducing a manufacturer to cancel planned work. The filing answers Apple's own trade-secrets suit against OpenAI, its io Products hardware unit and former Apple employees Chang Liu and Tang Tan, which is set for trial on July 19, 2027; Apple told CBS News the countersuit is an attempt to distract from the substance of its case, and OpenAI denies taking Apple's secrets.
items.plain: OpenAI is building a physical device, not just chatbots, and hardware needs factories - and the handful of factories that can do this precision work already build Apple's products. Apple sued first, saying OpenAI hired away its people and took its designs. OpenAI's answer flips it: Apple took OpenAI's files and leaned on those shared factories to slow OpenAI down, including by pushing its work to night shifts. A trade secret is just confidential know-how a company guards instead of patenting. Nothing has been proven; each side denies the other's claims.
items.why: The fight is over the contract manufacturers any new AI device has to pass through, which makes supplier access rather than model quality the chokepoint for OpenAI's hardware plans.

items.headline: Russia hits Ukraine's energy and rail network as Kyiv tables Black Sea ceasefire terms
items.body: Russian strikes hit civilian energy, fuel and transport infrastructure across nine Ukrainian regions on Friday, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky said, and Russia's Defence Ministry claimed on Saturday to have struck such targets in 156 areas, a claim not independently verified. Russia has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on Ukraine's energy system since September, and Ukraine has halted all electricity exports. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv has submitted Black Sea ceasefire proposals and is awaiting Russia's response, while Moscow has accepted European participation in a possible four-party round - Ukraine, the United States, Europe and Russia - in early December, with no date or venue set.
items.plain: Russia is less focused on taking ground right now than on switching off Ukraine's lights and heat going into winter. Power plants and the substations that move electricity are easy to hit and slow to rebuild, and Ukraine has stopped selling power abroad because it needs all of it at home. Meanwhile Ukraine has put a narrower offer on the table: stop shooting in the Black Sea, where grain ships sail, rather than everywhere at once. Russia has not replied. The 156 figure comes from Russia's own military, so treat it as a claim, not a count.
items.why: A Black Sea-only truce is the kind of partial deal both sides can sign without conceding territory, which makes it the likeliest first agreement to come out of the December talks.

items.headline: Black Friday online spending runs 12.8% ahead of last year
items.body: US shoppers spent $9.7 billion online by 6:30 p.m. ET on Black Friday, up 12.8% year on year, and Adobe Analytics raised its full-day estimate to between $13 billion and $13.4 billion, against $11.8 billion last year and its own September forecast of $12.9 billion. Salesforce, which tracks a different set of sites, counted $5.9 billion in US sales in the first half of the day and $30.7 billion globally, and projects $18.7 billion in the US for the day, up 4%. Adobe also reported a record $7.1 billion on Thanksgiving Day, up 10.4%, with mobile devices accounting for 63.2% of that spending, and forecasts $15.1 billion for Cyber Monday on November 30.
items.plain: These are not store receipts. Adobe watches checkout pages on retail websites and adds up dollars; Salesforce watches a different set of sites, which is why the two numbers differ so much. The part worth noticing is that spending is up about 13% while inflation runs near 3.8%, so people are genuinely buying more rather than just paying more. That matters because this is the first big holiday weekend with new tariffs raising the price of imported goods, and the early read says shoppers absorbed it. Final figures land later.
items.why: Consumer spending this strong removes the last argument against a Fed rate increase on December 9, which traders already price at better than 94%.

items.headline: CMS plan to cut $107 billion from Medicare Advantage bonuses reaches the Federal Register
items.body: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' proposed rule for contract year 2028 Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, released November 20, is scheduled to publish in the Federal Register today, opening the comment period. It would cut the Star Ratings system to 15 measures weighted toward clinical outcomes and patient experience, eliminate the "Reward Factor" that lifts plans sitting just below a bonus threshold, and change how bonuses are calculated - reducing payments to insurers by about $107 billion over ten years, by CMS's own estimate. CMS simulations show roughly 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments outright and about 58% of Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage scoring lower; UnitedHealth and Humana shares fell 19% and 16% in the week after the proposals, which also include a separate anti-fraud rule CMS projects will save $90 billion over a decade.
items.plain: More than half of people on Medicare now get it through a private insurer rather than from the government directly - that is Medicare Advantage. The government grades those plans one to five stars and pays a bonus to the high scorers, so stars are worth money, not just reputation. CMS wants to judge plans on fewer things, mostly whether patients actually got better, and to delete a rule that rounds borderline plans up. By CMS's own math, most plans that include drug coverage would score worse. This is a proposal: insurers get to comment, and will almost certainly sue.
items.why: Quality bonuses are where the margin in Medicare Advantage lives, so a cut this size shows up first as thinner extra benefits and fewer plan choices for seniors in 2028.

items.headline: Huang faces House questioning Tuesday over chip exports to China
items.body: Jensen Huang is scheduled to sit for a closed, transcribed interview on Tuesday with the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, which first requested his appearance in a November 12 letter warning that refusal would bring a subpoena; Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled the next day, and Huang is the only listed witness at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on export controls on December 3. The schedule survived his reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive on November 23, which the board said followed "input from senior levels of the United States government" and which Trump said he influenced "directly and indirectly." A House Intelligence spokesperson said the reinstatement "changes nothing"; Republican senators Kevin Cramer, John Curtis, Pete Ricketts and Tom Cotton criticized it, and Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi cited Nvidia's $25 million donation to the White House ballroom project.
items.plain: Nvidia makes the chips that AI runs on, and US law restricts selling the best ones to China. Huang was out as chief executive, then back three weeks later after the White House weighed in with the company's board, which is unusual: presidents do not normally help pick who runs a public company. Congress separately wants to know whether Nvidia chips have been reaching China anyway, routed through other countries or rented out as computing time. A "transcribed interview" is private questioning with a written record lawmakers can quote later. Republicans, not only Democrats, are the ones objecting.
items.why: Putting Nvidia's China exposure into a congressional transcript rather than a press story is what turns export-control complaints into subpoenas and legislation.

items.headline: Japan orders Chinese ships away from a fishing boat near disputed islands
items.body: Japan's coast guard said two Chinese government vessels approached a Japanese fishing boat in waters near the Senkaku islands, which China calls the Diaoyu, and that it repeatedly warned them to leave - the fifth time this year a Chinese vessel has approached a Japanese fishing boat there, by the coast guard's count. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing had lodged "serious representations" with Tokyo. Relations have been at their lowest in years since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told the Diet in November 2025 that a Taiwan contingency could be a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, after which China curbed tourism to Japan and banned Japanese seafood imports.
items.plain: The Senkakus are five uninhabited islands that Japan administers and China claims. Neither country wants a war over rocks, so the dispute is fought with ships: coast guard vessels shadow fishing boats, each side radios the other to leave, and both file protests. This is the fifth such approach this year, and the pattern is the message. The deeper quarrel is Taiwan - Japan's prime minister said last year that an attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival, which in Japanese law is the phrase that permits fighting alongside an ally. Beijing has punished Japan economically ever since.
items.why: Each repetition raises the odds of a collision between armed government ships, which is how a quarrel over uninhabited rocks becomes a test of the US-Japan security treaty.

items.headline: Tokyo core inflation hits 2.9%, the fastest in 16 months
items.body: Core consumer prices in Tokyo, which exclude fresh food, rose 2.9% in November from a year earlier, Japan's Statistics Bureau reported Friday - up from 2.6% in October and the fastest pace in 16 months, but below the 3.0% economists expected. Headline inflation held at 2.8%, while the measure excluding both fresh food and energy slowed to 2.5%, its weakest in three months. Part of the core increase reflects the expiry of government utility subsidies, which lowered the year-earlier base rather than raising current prices; the Bank of Japan's policy board meets December 17 and 18.
items.plain: Tokyo's price data arrives about three weeks before the national figures, so economists treat it as an early look. Core inflation leaves out fresh food because vegetable prices swing with the weather and drown out the trend. The 2.9% looks alarming until you see why: the government was subsidising electricity and gas bills a year ago, so last year's prices were artificially low, which makes this year's look high by comparison. The measure that ignores energy altogether actually slowed. So the number argues for a rate rise, but less strongly than the headline suggests.
items.why: Japan still has the world's cheapest money, and every Bank of Japan increase pulls Japanese savings home out of foreign bond markets, raising borrowing costs elsewhere.

items.headline: Canada takes its AI compute fund to C$1 billion and ties the biggest subsidies to Canadian ownership
items.body: Canada added C$700 million to its AI Compute Access Fund, bringing the total to C$1 billion, on top of the original C$300 million committed under its Sovereign AI Compute Strategy. The fund will now cover up to 80% of eligible compute costs bought from a "sovereign" provider - one incorporated in Canada with ultimate Canadian ownership and decision-making that runs its infrastructure and processes data in Canada - and up to 50% from other Canadian-based providers, with compute hosted outside Canada ineligible. It targets projects with compute costs of roughly C$100,000 to C$5 million, mainly small and medium-sized firms, runs through March 2030, and opens with a call for health and life sciences; Budget 2026 separately committed to bringing 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute online.
items.plain: Training an AI model means renting time on racks of expensive chips, and almost all of those racks belong to American companies. Canada is offering to pay most of the bill, but only if a Canadian company rents Canadian-owned machines sitting on Canadian soil. Rent from a US cloud and you get nothing. The reasoning is partly jobs and partly law: data on servers in another country can be reached by that country's government. The catch is that Canada does not yet have much of this capacity, which is why the same budget promises to build 500 megawatts of it.
items.why: Tying subsidies to ownership and location rather than price is the mechanism by which "sovereign AI" stops being rhetoric and starts splitting the cloud market along national lines.

sources.outlet: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada

items.headline: Hackers breached the Air Force's main cloud platform
items.body: Hackers broke into Cloud One, the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, Reuters reported Friday, citing three people familiar with the matter; one said the attackers exploited a software flaw to reach the platform's control plane, the administrative layer used to manage cloud resources. The intrusion was discovered within the past month during system upgrades. Cloud One hosts the Cloud-Based Command and Control system, which collates North American air defense radar feeds, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force locations; updates to applications running on it were blocked, leaving personnel unable to apply fixes. An Air Force spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny the breach, operator Leidos referred questions to the Air Force, and Reuters could not establish who the hackers are, how far they got, or whether data was taken.
items.plain: Cloud One is where the Air Force runs its software instead of owning the servers itself. The control plane is the master switchboard - not the files, but the panel that decides who may see and change them, which is why reaching it is worse than reaching any single application. Two things living there matter most: one feeds radar pictures of North American airspace, the other is the inventory list for bombs and missiles at over 200 bases. Nobody has said what was taken, and the Air Force will not confirm the break-in. The known damage so far is that patching stopped.
items.why: Knowing where munitions are stored is an intelligence prize on its own, whether or not anything was destroyed or altered.

items.headline: Trump told deployed troops victory in Iran will come "whenever I want it to be"
items.body: On a Thanksgiving call to deployed troops from Mar-a-Lago on November 26, Trump told a service member, "You're going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand," and when asked when that victory would arrive said it would come "sort of whenever I want it to be." The war with Iran is in its ninth month; Pentagon deputy comptroller Arthur Miller told the Senate Armed Services Committee that its cost had reached $48.3 billion as of November 13, up from about $47 billion in October, a figure that excludes repairs to US bases damaged in the fighting, which lawmakers have requested and not received. Trump told the New York Post this week that operations are funded through late January and acknowledged that the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could constrain him; he gave the troops no timetable for coming home.
items.plain: American troops have been fighting Iran for nine months. On a holiday call home, one of them effectively asked the president when it ends, and the answer was that he will decide - and that victory is already "at hand." Two numbers sit against that. The Pentagon's own accountant told the Senate the war has cost $48.3 billion so far, and that total leaves out repairing the American bases Iran hit, which Congress has asked for and not been given. Trump also said the money runs out in late January, the same month a Congress controlled by the other party arrives.
items.why: Funding expires in late January and the Congress that must renew it changes hands that month, so "whenever I want it to be" describes a decision he may no longer control.
